title: Transferable safety constraints built into socio-technical systems

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reusable engineering method that connects hazard analysis to implemented safety constraints and continuing evidence that those constraints work. It would help designers specify the conditions and behaviors needed to prevent or contain defined hazards, incorporate those constraints into equipment, software, human responsibilities and organizational controls, and maintain their effectiveness throughout operation. Transferability would require independent teams to obtain convincing results across substantially different systems using a common method.

Its technical foundation is a system-level view of safety. Dangerous outcomes can arise through interactions among functioning components, people, software and organizations. System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) examines control structures, unsafe control actions and scenarios that can produce losses. Its outputs can inform functional requirements, architecture and test plans. The proposed capability extends this pathway through demonstrably effective implementation and sustained operational assurance.

Every assurance would have a defined scope, including the losses and hazards considered, system boundaries, operating conditions and assumptions about people, equipment and the environment. Changes in those conditions would require reassessment. The concept belongs to industrial engineering through socio-technical system design and lifecycle safety, with contributions from systems engineering, control engineering, human factors, reliability engineering and software verification.

significance.text: A transferable method could make architectural protection more systematic across industrial and service systems. Designers could use identified hazardous interactions to shape control authority, feedback, requirements and testing early in development. STPA already describes this architectural role. The prospective advance is reliable execution of that role across settings, accompanied by evidence that the resulting constraints remain effective.

Conditional impact assessment. If the method substantially reduced serious hazards across different settings, it could shift more protection into system architecture and reduce dependence on training and after-the-fact detection. Reusable assurance practices could also help teams assess the safety implications of equipment replacement, software updates and organizational changes. These downstream benefits would depend on the quality of implementation, the coverage of the analysis and the resources available to maintain the controls.

Comparison with major historical changes in industrial safety practice is an evaluative analogy whose force would depend on demonstrated risk reduction and broad adoption. Claims of effectiveness would remain bounded by specified hazards, operating envelopes and assumptions. Unknown hazards, incomplete models, degradation and changing organizational conditions would continue to create residual risk.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is a transferable, verifiable transition from interaction-based hazard analysis to enforceable and maintainable safety constraints. Analysts must turn unsafe control actions and loss scenarios into precise requirements, allocate those requirements to the people and technical elements capable of enforcing them, and show that the implemented system satisfies them. The NASA aircraft study gives a concrete example of this translation difficulty. Its authors reported that the STPA Handbook did not directly guide their transition from analysis results to finalized requirements, and their work left the constraint set incomplete. This is evidence from one team's experience, influenced in part by resource limitations.

Analysis boundaries and traceability are substantial engineering barriers. A team must include interactions that materially affect safety, connect unsafe control actions to higher-level hazards, and preserve those links through requirements and verification. The NASA application reported additional risks when boundaries expanded, while omitting explicit links from unsafe control actions to higher-level hazards. Its limited independent comparison also left questions about the additional value of the analysis unresolved. Prioritization and verification require further work, and the authors found insufficient evidence that STPA could fully replace the approaches serving those functions in their application.

Continuing assurance must account for change. Control algorithms can become inadequate as system conditions change, and sensors and actuators can degrade. Human responsibilities, organizational practices and operating environments can also evolve. A practical method must identify when its assumptions have weakened and support reassessment of the affected constraints. The supplied sources establish mechanisms that motivate this requirement, while leaving the difficulty and effectiveness of a general operational solution unquantified.

Engineering synthesis. Transferability adds a further challenge because different domains have different hazards, control structures, evidence and operational constraints. A common method would need to preserve enough specificity to produce enforceable requirements while remaining reproducible across those differences. Demonstrating its practical value would also require credible comparisons with existing safety engineering and explicit accounting for analysis effort, implementation burden and maintenance costs.

current_state.text: Nancy G. Leveson and John P. Thomas's March 2018 STPA Handbook documents a structured process for defining losses, hazards and system-level constraints, modeling control structures, identifying unsafe control actions and developing loss scenarios. It connects analysis outputs to requirements, architecture and testing. The supplied review examined a truncated extraction covering pages 1–50. Although the earlier research cited Chapter 3 around page 59, inspected earlier pages independently support these methodological claims.

The supplied research identifies the FAA report Evaluation of System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) for Improving Aviation Safety, attributed to John P. Thomas and John G. Van Houdt, as DOT/FAA/TC-24/16, dated 1 July 2024. The research says its repository description discussed aviation applications, benefits, limitations and hands-on work. The source index retains no artifact for this citation, and the validated review had no source text with which to verify that account or assess the report's findings. Its substantive conclusions therefore remain unverified within the supplied evidence.

A 2026 NASA study by Matthew P. Huffman, James M. Green and Tinicia J. Menifee applied STPA to an early hybrid-electric aircraft concept, focusing on its energy storage system and electric powertrain. The repository lists a meeting on August 17–20, 2026. The team reported that expanding the analysis boundaries could expose additional risks and suggested that rigorous traditional methods using broader boundaries might obtain similar results. That suggestion requires qualification because the independent hazard-analysis comparison was limited.

The NASA application remained preliminary. It left the full constraint set undeveloped, omitted explicit links between unsafe control actions and higher-level hazards, and completed only a limited independent comparison. Its authors identified unresolved prioritization and verification needs. These details constrain what the study establishes about completed safety requirements, comparative performance and operational effectiveness. The validated review used prose spanning all 19 pages of the paper, with no declared text truncation. Figure images were uninspected, so figure-dependent interpretations remain outside that assessment.

Evidence-scope synthesis. The supplied materials establish an existing analysis method and an early aircraft application. Cross-system transferability, sustained operational assurance and substantial realized risk reduction remain to be demonstrated in this record. No bounded freshness search was supplied, so the materials cannot establish the field-wide state as of 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Independent teams would apply a common design and assurance method to several substantially different high-consequence systems. Before deployment, each team would specify the losses, hazards, system boundaries, operating envelope, assumptions and measurable safety constraints. The demonstration plan would define what counts as a substantially different system and justify the selected range of applications. These are proposed evidentiary requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams apply a common method across substantially different high-consequence systems

completion_criteria.text: Proposed implementation evidence. Each application would preserve traceability from hazards through unsafe control actions and loss scenarios to finalized requirements, implemented controls and verification results. Independent review and fault injection or other realistic testing would examine whether the constraints prevent or contain specified hazardous scenarios, including foreseeable human and equipment failures. Testing would address relevant timing, feedback, degradation and operating-context assumptions. This proposal responds to the documented transition and verification gaps.
completion_criteria.label: Hazard-traceable implemented constraints prevent or contain specified hazardous scenarios

completion_criteria.text: Proposed effectiveness evidence. Prospective operating observations and comparison with credible existing safety engineering would assess risk reduction and continued constraint effectiveness. Before execution, teams would define the sampling approach, safety metrics, observation periods, uncertainty treatment and the improvement needed to justify a claim of substantial benefit. Reports would disclose residual risk, missed hazards, constraint violations, implementation effort and maintenance costs. The supplied sources provide no established numerical thresholds for these proposals.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective comparisons assess risk reduction and continued constraint effectiveness

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries. Independent teams would need sufficient access to the method, assumptions, analysis records and verification procedures to reproduce the reasoning and evaluate the results. Demonstrations would examine how assurance is maintained when equipment, software, organizational responsibilities or operating conditions change. Finite applications and tests would establish demonstrated breadth within their stated conditions. Any broader claim would require additional evidence, with the boundaries of each assurance made explicit.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce assurance reasoning within explicit demonstrated boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. IND-01, General-purpose, rapidly reconfigurable production, overlaps through the safety implications of changing production configurations. Transferable safety constraints could help govern permitted reconfigurations and reassessment after change. IND-01 concerns production flexibility, while IND-06 concerns safety constraint design and assurance across socio-technical systems.

Roster-based synthesis. IND-02, Production-time qualification of individual critical parts, could provide evidence relevant to equipment assumptions and component-related hazards. Its focus is the qualification of individual parts. IND-06 addresses system-level interactions, including control, software, human and organizational contributions to safety.

Roster-based synthesis. IND-03, A predictive and testable science of supply-network cascade containment, shares an interest in interacting systems and the containment of harmful propagation. Supply-network predictions could inform hazards and constraints in a networked operation. IND-03 centers on supply-network cascades, while IND-06 centers on transferable safety engineering and lifecycle assurance.

Roster-based synthesis. IND-04, Economical mixed-product disassembly and recovery, offers a potential application setting in which changing products, equipment and worker interactions would require safety controls. Its central objective is economical recovery. IND-06 would address the definition, implementation and maintenance of safety constraints within such operations.

Roster-based synthesis. IND-05, Transferable prediction and prevention of work-related human performance risk, has close overlap through human actions, working conditions and organizational influences. Its predictions and interventions could inform safety requirements. IND-06 spans the wider control structure connecting people, software, equipment and organizations, including hazardous interactions involving functioning components.

unresolved_issues: The FAA report's substantive contents remain unverified because no source artifact was retained.
The handbook extraction ends at page 50, leaving the originally cited Chapter 3 passage around page 59 outside the reviewed material.
The NASA paper's figure images were uninspected, leaving figure-dependent details unassessed.
The supplied record does not establish the field-wide state as of 1 November 2026 because no bounded freshness search was provided.
The breadth of cross-system transferability, sustained operational effectiveness and comparative risk reduction remains unestablished in the supplied evidence.
A future demonstration must define system diversity, sampling, metrics, observation periods, uncertainty thresholds and acceptable implementation and maintenance burdens.
